title: Deprecating the "X-" Prefix and Similar Constructs in Application Protocols
summary: Protocol designers once marked experimental parameters with an X- prefix. This best current practice says that convention causes more problems than it solves and deprecates it for newly defined parameters with textual names in application protocols.

eli5.summary: Experimental names used to get a special label. But names stuck around after becoming real, so the label caused trouble and is no longer recommended.

questions: why is the x- prefix deprecated
should i prefix custom http headers with x-
subtitle: Why new protocol parameters should stop being named with an X- prefix, and what to do instead.

tldr.problem: Protocols long marked unstandardized parameters with an "X-" prefix, but parameters that proved useful leaked into the standard space and the prefix then had to be supported forever.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC deprecates the "X-" convention for newly defined parameters with textual names, and tells implementers, parameter creators and protocol designers what to do without it.
tldr.outcome: New parameters should get meaningful, probably unused names and a registration, and nobody should infer a parameter's status from an "X-" in its name.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Newly defined parameters with textual names

facts.label: Implementers
facts.value: MUST NOT infer status from an X- prefix

today: RFC 6648 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 178) and the metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It records the guidance that new textual parameters should not use an X- prefix, while leaving existing X- parameters to their maintainers.

sections.title: The "X-" Convention and Its Deprecation
sections.content:
Many application protocols use parameters with textual names (as opposed to numbers) to identify data: media types, header fields in Internet mail and HTTP requests, vCard parameters and properties, and so on. Historically, designers marked unstandardized parameters by prefixing the name with X- or a similar construct such as x.. The "X" is commonly understood to mean "eXperimental" or "eXtension".

In theory this avoided collisions between standardized and unstandardized names. In practice, the RFC says, the benefits have been outweighed by the costs of unstandardized parameters leaking into the standards space. So it deprecates the convention for newly defined parameters in application protocols, including new parameters for established protocols, even where the convention was only implicit.

The scope is deliberately narrow. The RFC does not recommend against private, local, preliminary, experimental or implementation-specific parameters, only against using X- in their names. It makes no recommendation on whether existing X- parameters should be migrated, and it does not override specifications that require X-, such as the x-name token in iCalendar.
sections.eli5: The old habit was to stick a special sticker on test names. This document says new names should not get that sticker, but it does not tell anyone to peel off old stickers.

sections.title: Where the Convention Came From
sections.content:
The convention goes back to 1975, when a suggestion about FTP parameters proposed that an initial letter X be used for "really local idiosyncracies". The X prefix was then used in RFC 737, RFC 743 and RFC 775, and RFC 1123 noted that FTP allows experimental commands whose names begin with "X".

For email header fields, RFC 822 (1982) reserved X- for user-defined fields and said it would never be used for standard extension fields. The convention then spread to media types, HTTP headers, vCard, Uniform Resource Names and LDAP field names. Yet email's distinction was effectively removed by RFC 2822 in 2001, and a similar change happened for the SIP P- headers when RFC 5727 obsoleted RFC 3427.

Two situations motivate continued use: experiments that might be standardized if they succeed, and extensions meant only for implementation-specific or private-network use. The RFC notes that the Internet Standards Process and IANA registration rules do not mandate the convention. It is a choice made by each specification or administrative process, and some Standards Track RFCs have treated it normatively.
sections.eli5: The sticker idea started with a small suggestion about file-sharing commands and slowly spread to email, web and other systems. Later, email stopped treating the sticker as meaningful.

sections.title: Rules for Implementers and Parameter Creators
sections.content:
Implementers of application protocols MUST NOT assume anything about a parameter's status, or take automatic action on it, based only on whether its name has X- or a similar construct.

Creators of new parameters:

  • SHOULD assume that every parameter they create might become standardized, public, commonly deployed or usable across multiple implementations.
  • SHOULD choose meaningful names that they have reason to believe are currently unused.
  • SHOULD NOT prefix names with X- or similar constructs.

If a name space has conventions that tie names to their creators, a name may include the organization's name or primary domain name.
sections.eli5: If you invent a new name, pick a clear one nobody else is using, and assume it may become popular. Do not rely on a sticker to tell people how serious it is.

sections.title: Rules for Protocol Designers
sections.content:
Designers of new application protocols that allow extension through parameters:

  • SHOULD establish registries with potentially unlimited value spaces, defining both permanent and provisional registries if appropriate.
  • SHOULD define simple, clear registration procedures.
  • SHOULD mandate registration of all non-private parameters, whatever the form of the name.
  • SHOULD NOT prohibit parameters with an X- prefix from being registered.
  • MUST NOT say that a parameter with X- must be understood as unstandardized, or that one without it must be understood as standardized.

The idea is that easy registration removes the old reason for separate name spaces, which was the perceived difficulty of registering names.
sections.eli5: People who design new systems should make it easy to sign up a new name in a big list. And they should never say that a name with a sticker is automatically "not official".

sections.title: Why the Prefix Causes Problems
sections.content:
The main problem is leakage. Once an X- parameter becomes useful, it must migrate to a standardized name. Older implementations only know the X- name and newer ones may only know the new one, so newer implementations keep supporting the X- name forever. The unstandardized name has then become a de facto standard, which defeats the point of segregating the name space.

The RFC gives examples. FTP implementations were told to recognize both forms of experimental commands. HTTP treats x-gzip and x-compress as equivalent to gzip and compress. RFC 5064 defines Archived-At but also had to describe the X-Archived-At precursor, which may be parsed but should not be generated.

There is also a security angle: a standardized version may differ subtly, for example in security properties after review, so treating the old and new names as identical can cause interoperability and security problems.

The RFC accepts that segregating names can be justified in a few cases: parameters that will almost certainly never be standardized (use an organization or domain name, or even a nonsense word, hash or UUID), names that carry significant meaning, and very short names where numbers with a private-use range are better. It also answers three objections, including that RFC 3692 (BCP 82) favours experimental numbers: that advice concerns limited number pools, whereas text-name spaces are not limited.
sections.eli5: When a test name becomes popular, old and new programs need both names, so you end up with two names forever. A good clear name from the start avoids that mess.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security section says that interoperability and migration problems with security-critical parameters can create unnecessary vulnerabilities. As a corollary of the rule for implementers, implementations MUST NOT assume that standardized parameters are "secure" and unstandardized ones "insecure" based solely on their names.

On the IANA side, the document does not change any registration procedures now in force. Such procedures might be updated in the future to adopt the best practices it describes.
sections.eli5: A name does not tell you whether something is safe. You have to look at what it does, not at whether it has a sticker.
